confirmed: Read the complete local markdown and all 11 PDF pages, including references; the PDF is the Proceedings of the Design Society, Volume 6: DESIGN 2026 article, printed pp. 2161–2171, DOI 10.1017/pds.2026.10574. Title and authors match the form (PDF p. 1); no appendix or supplementary-material reference is present in this document.

The paper reports one comparison of AI-assisted and human-only workshops in different classes, with different themes and participants; no random allocation is described. quasi_people, observational context and exclusion from the randomized core are supported (PDF p. 2, Section 2.1; PDF p. 10, Section 4, limitations).

The analyzed survey sample is 88 people: A has 43 retained responses from 54 workshop participants, and B has 45 from 104; these are not randomized counts. Across arms the sample exceeds 50 people (PDF p. 5, Table 3 and Table 6 heading).

Idea evaluation used 19 retained groups in A and 15 in B, from 19 and 25 groups respectively. These group counts must remain distinct from people counts; the paper does not explain the mapping of group outputs to the participant-count tests, and novelty/usability rows give df=84 without outcome-specific arm counts (PDF p. 4, Section 2.3; PDF p. 5, Tables 3 and 6).

The participants were economics and management undergraduates; workshops lasted 90 minutes and were conducted in Japanese, using New Space Hotel Business in A and New Food Business in B (PDF p. 2, Section 2.1; PDF p. 4, Section 2.3).

The tablet application generated follow-up interview questions, alternative HMW statements and up to six brainstorming ideas; teams selected three ideas from human and AI suggestions. Figure 2 labels the model Chat GPT4.0 LLM (PDF p. 3, Section 2.2, Table 1 and Figure 2, inspected in memory).

Fluency counts brainstorming post-its. Novelty and usability use average scores for three selected ideas on a 5-point scale, rated by five external evaluators: two senior designers, one professional engineer and two bachelor’s students (PDF p. 4, Section 2.3 and Table 2).
Idea-count statistics match exactly: A M=11.05, SD=4.705; B M=15.40, SD=8.606; t(86)=−2.925, p=.004, Cohen’s d=.63 as printed (PDF p. 5, Table 6).
Novelty statistics match exactly: A M=2.9721, SD=.42619; B M=3.1783, SD=.37508; t(84)=−2.382, p=.019, Cohen’s d=.52 as printed (PDF p. 5, Table 6).
Usability statistics match exactly: A M=3.6946, SD=.28812; B M=3.1348, SD=.52785; t(84)=6.103, p<.001, Cohen’s d=1.33 as printed (PDF p. 5, Table 6).

The one-line finding accurately reports Table 6: the AI workshop had fewer ideas, lower novelty and higher usability. The form correctly flags the contradictory sentence about fewer ideas in human-only teams in the conclusion (PDF p. 5, Section 3.2 and Table 6; PDF p. 9, Section 4).

This is an original workshop study, not a synthesis; no pooled estimates require checking. The other creativity scales are self-reports, and qualitative comments are participants’ perceptions rather than scored output diversity (PDF pp. 4–8, Sections 2.3 and 3.1–3.3).
summary: The full proceedings article supports the quasi-experimental/observational classification, retained sample of 88 people, and all three reported output comparisons; no randomized people study is reported. Corrections are needed for the omitted exclusion criteria and the incorrectly denied company involvement.
